stages.title: Systems biology
stages.hook: A bacterium swims up a nutrient gradient with a few thousand proteins and no brain. Why can a network of simple interactions behave in ways no single component predicts?
explain: Systems biology studies how interacting components (genes, proteins, metabolites) give rise to behaviour of the whole. Models describe networks with ordinary differential equations. For a protein made at rate k_syn and degraded with first-order rate constant k_deg, dX/dt = k_syn − k_deg·X. The steady state is X_ss = k_syn ÷ k_deg, and the half-life is ln 2 ÷ k_deg.

Network motifs recur in biology. Negative feedback stabilises levels and speeds responses; with delay it can produce oscillations (circadian clocks). Positive feedback with cooperativity can produce bistability and switch-like decisions with hysteresis, as in cell-fate choices. Feed-forward loops filter out brief noisy inputs. Cooperative binding is often described by a Hill function: response = Sⁿ ÷ (Kⁿ + Sⁿ), where n measures steepness.

Genome-scale metabolic models use flux balance analysis: at steady state, the stoichiometric matrix S times flux vector v equals zero (S·v = 0), and a linear programme finds fluxes that optimise an objective such as growth. Stochastic effects matter when molecules are few: gene expression is noisy even in genetically identical cells. Models need data to constrain parameters and are tested by predicting new experiments.

example.q: A protein is made at 10 nM/min and degraded with k_deg = 0.2 per min. Find the steady-state concentration and half-life.

analogies.city: Traffic jams emerge from the interactions of many cars, though no single car causes them.
analogies.tech: A thermostat plus heater is a negative feedback loop, and a latching switch is a bistable circuit.
analogies.music: A chord is more than its notes: the interactions give the harmony.

stages.mnemonic: Parts list is not the machine: connections create behaviour.
terms: A state where production and removal balance so concentrations stay constant.
Existence of two stable states for the same conditions.
A parameter describing the steepness of a cooperative response.
Method predicting metabolic fluxes under a steady-state constraint.

misc.wrong: A model that fits the data is therefore correct.
misc.right: Several different models can fit the same data; a model gains credibility by correctly predicting new, independent experiments.

stages.limits: Parameters are often poorly measured, and models omit most of the cell's components, so predictions beyond the tested range are uncertain.

trip.prompt: Find an example of a genetic oscillator and say what feedback produces the cycle.

questions.q: Which network feature is required for a cell-fate decision to remember its past state (hysteresis)?
o: Positive feedback with ultrasensitivity
Pure negative feedback with fast decay
A simple linear pathway with no loops
No feedback of any kind in the network
questions.why: Positive feedback produces bistability and memory.

questions.q: A negative feedback loop with a long delay is most likely to produce:
o: Oscillations
A permanent switch
No dynamics
Linear growth
questions.why: Delayed negative feedback overshoots and oscillates.

questions.q: A protein is produced at 6 nM/min and degraded with k_deg = 0.03 per min. What is the steady-state concentration in nM?
Using response = Sⁿ ÷ (Kⁿ + Sⁿ) with n = 2 and K = 10, find the response at S = 20 (as a fraction).
A feed-forward loop requires both direct and indirect (delayed) activation to turn on a gene. What does it filter out?
o: Brief spurious input pulses
Sustained signals lasting a long time
All signals, including brief ones, without delay
Transcription of every gene in the network
questions.why: The delay means only persistent input activates the target.

questions.q: In flux balance analysis, which assumption lets the system be solved as S·v = 0?
o: Metabolite concentrations are at steady state
All the fluxes in the network are equal
All the enzymes are fully saturated
There is no growth in any of the cells
questions.why: Steady state means production equals consumption for each internal metabolite.

questions.q: Order the cycle of building and testing a systems model.
questions.why: Models are iterated against experiments.

questions.q: Match each motif to its typical function.
questions.why: Motifs have characteristic behaviours.

questions.q: Two genetically identical bacteria in the same medium show very different levels of a protein. Give two reasons.
questions.model: Gene expression is stochastic when few molecules are involved, so identical cells vary by chance. Positive feedback can also lock cells into different stable states, and cell-cycle stage or history may differ.
questions.why: Noise and bistability create cell-to-cell variation.

questions.q: Genetically identical bacteria in the same medium show different protein levels. Which feature of gene expression best explains this?
o: Stochastic fluctuations when few molecules are involved
A new mutation arises in every cell
The cells have different genomes
Transcription is completely absent in some of them
questions.why: Randomness in transcription and translation causes cell-to-cell variability.

panel.q: A model with 15 free parameters fits the training data perfectly but fails on new data. This is probably:
o: Overfitting
Underfitting
A correct model
A deterministic result
panel.why: Too much flexibility captures noise rather than mechanism.

panel.q: A drug targets one enzyme in a pathway, but the cell compensates through an alternative route. Which concept is shown?
o: Network robustness and redundancy
A feed-forward loop that filters brief pulses
Enzyme saturation at high substrate
Mass action kinetics in solution
panel.why: Redundant routes buffer against single-node perturbations.

panel.q: Doubling the degradation rate constant of a protein at constant synthesis rate will:
o: Halve the steady-state level and halve the half-life
Double the steady-state level and halve the half-life
Not change the level or the half-life at all
Halve the steady-state level but double the half-life
panel.why: X_ss = k_syn ÷ k_deg falls by half; t½ = ln 2 ÷ k_deg also halves.

teach.topic: Why feedback matters in cell networks
teach.model: Negative feedback makes an output push itself back toward a set level, which stabilises it, and with a delay it can make regular oscillations. Positive feedback amplifies a change, so a system can flip between two stable states, like a switch that remembers. Many cell decisions rely on these loops.

points.ask: Can you give an example of a behaviour that results?

stages.title: Advanced molecular biology
stages.hook: The same gene can make several different proteins, and a short RNA can silence a gene. How does a cell control information after the DNA is written?
explain: Gene expression is regulated at many levels. In bacteria, operons are controlled by repressors and activators: the lac operon is induced when lactose is present and glucose is low, because the repressor is released from the operator by allolactose and the activator CAP–cAMP promotes transcription. In eukaryotes, enhancers bind transcription factors that recruit the Mediator complex and RNA polymerase II to the promoter. Chromatin state matters: DNA wraps about 1.65 times around histone octamers, about 147 bp per nucleosome, and histone acetylation generally opens chromatin while certain methylation marks compact it.

RNA processing adds a 5′ cap and a poly-A tail and splices introns. Alternative splicing allows one gene to produce multiple mRNA variants. Non-coding RNAs regulate: microRNAs and siRNAs guide the RNA-induced silencing complex to complementary mRNAs, causing degradation or translational repression (RNA interference). Translation is controlled at initiation, and protein stability is controlled by ubiquitin tagging and the proteasome.

Methods: RT-qPCR measures RNA with the cycle threshold (Ct), the cycle at which fluorescence passes a threshold; a lower Ct means more starting template. With efficiency near 100%, fold change = 2^(−ΔΔCt). ChIP-seq maps DNA–protein binding; RNA-seq measures transcripts; CRISPR screens test gene function at scale.

example.q: In qPCR, a treated sample has ΔCt (target − reference) of 2.0 and the control has ΔCt of 5.0. What is the fold change in target expression, treated versus control?

analogies.tech: Splicing is video editing: the same footage can be cut into different versions.
analogies.city: Enhancers are like distant billboards that recruit crowds to a shop.
analogies.music: RNA interference is a mute button on a particular instrument.

stages.mnemonic: Cap, cut, tail, test: 5′ cap, splice, poly-A tail, then quality control.
terms: A DNA element that increases transcription of a gene, sometimes from far away.
Joining exons in different combinations to make different mRNAs.
Gene silencing by small RNAs guided to complementary mRNAs.
The cycle at which qPCR fluorescence crosses a threshold.

misc.right: Alternative splicing, alternative promoters and processing let one gene encode many protein variants; in humans most multi-exon genes are alternatively spliced.

stages.limits: Correlation of RNA and protein levels is often moderate, so mRNA abundance alone is an imperfect proxy for protein activity.

trip.prompt: Find the conditions under which the lac operon is on, and say what the repressor and CAP each do.

questions.q: The lac operon is transcribed at a high rate when:
o: Lactose is present and glucose is absent
Lactose and glucose are both abundant in the medium
Glucose is present and lactose is absent
Neither sugar is present in the medium
questions.why: Allolactose releases the repressor and low glucose raises cAMP, activating CAP.

questions.q: A mutation prevents the lac repressor from binding the operator. What is the result?
o: Constitutive expression of the operon
No expression of the operon, ever
Expression only when glucose is present
Loss of the lac genes from the DNA
questions.why: Without the repressor, RNA polymerase is not blocked.

questions.q: What is the main outcome when siRNA binds a perfectly complementary mRNA in RISC?
o: The mRNA is cleaved
The DNA is mutated
The ribosome is duplicated
The mRNA is capped
questions.why: Argonaute cleaves target RNA with high complementarity.

questions.q: In qPCR, ΔCt for treated cells is 3 and for control cells is 6. By what fold is the target higher in treated cells (2^(−ΔΔCt))?
A haploid human genome has 3.2 × 10⁹ bp. If nucleosomes are spaced every 200 bp, about how many nucleosomes are there (in millions)?
Histone acetylation at a promoter generally leads to:
o: More open chromatin and higher transcription
Gene deletion from the chromosome
Higher DNA methylation at the promoter
Lower splicing of the mRNA in the nucleus
questions.why: Acetylation neutralises positive charge on histones, loosening DNA contact.

questions.q: Order the steps from gene to functional protein in a eukaryote.
questions.why: mRNA processing precedes export and translation.

questions.q: Match each technique to what it measures.
questions.why: Each method answers a different question.

questions.q: A gene's mRNA level doubles after treatment, but its protein level does not change. Give two possible explanations.
questions.model: Translation may be repressed (for example by microRNAs), or the protein may be degraded faster via ubiquitin–proteasome. It could also be a timing delay, or feedback offsetting the change.
questions.why: mRNA level is only one control point.

questions.q: An mRNA with a poly-A tail and 5′ cap is exported to the cytoplasm. Which role do these features mainly serve?
o: Stability and efficient translation
Cutting introns out of the pre-mRNA
Starting DNA replication in the nucleus
Opening up the chromatin around the gene
questions.why: The cap and tail protect mRNA from degradation and help ribosome recruitment.

panel.q: Enhancers can act at a distance of tens of kilobases. What structural feature explains this?
o: DNA looping brings them close to the promoter
RNA carries signals along the DNA strand
Enhancers are translated into proteins that travel
DNA is perfectly straight, so they simply slide
panel.why: Chromatin looping allows distant elements to contact promoters.

panel.q: A tumour suppresses a microRNA that normally represses an oncogene mRNA. What is expected?
o: Higher oncogene protein levels
Lower oncogene protein levels in the cell
No change in the oncogene protein
Deletion of the oncogene from the genome
panel.why: Loss of repression increases translation or stability.

panel.q: Why must qPCR use a reference gene?
o: To normalise for differences in input RNA and efficiency
To amplify the target gene more strongly
To replace the primers during the run
To count the number of nucleosomes present
panel.why: Normalisation controls for sample-to-sample variation.

teach.topic: How a cell controls gene expression after transcription
teach.model: A new RNA is capped, spliced and given a poly-A tail. Alternative splicing can make different proteins from one gene. Small RNAs such as microRNAs can bind mRNAs and block translation or cause degradation. Finally, proteins can be tagged with ubiquitin and destroyed by the proteasome.

points.ask: What happens to the RNA first?
How can small RNAs regulate genes?

stages.title: Structural biology
stages.hook: A protein chain of 300 amino acids folds into one precise shape in milliseconds to seconds, though it could adopt astronomically many shapes. How do we see that shape, and why does it matter?
explain: Protein structure has four levels: primary (amino acid sequence), secondary (α-helices and β-sheets stabilised by backbone hydrogen bonds), tertiary (overall 3D fold) and quaternary (arrangement of several chains). Folding is driven largely by the hydrophobic effect, which buries nonpolar side chains in the core, with hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, van der Waals forces and disulfide bonds adding stability. Levinthal's paradox notes that a random search of all conformations would take too long, so folding must follow guided pathways down an energy funnel. Chaperones help some proteins fold.

X-ray crystallography passes X-rays through a crystal; diffraction follows Bragg's law: nλ = 2d·sin θ. Electron density maps are built from diffraction intensities, but the phase problem must be solved. Cryo-electron microscopy images flash-frozen molecules and now reaches near-atomic resolution for large complexes without crystals. NMR gives structures in solution for small proteins and reveals dynamics. Resolution is quoted in ångström (1 Å = 0.1 nm).

Computational methods such as AlphaFold predict structures from sequence with high accuracy for many proteins, but predictions can be unreliable for flexible regions, complexes and the effects of mutations. Structure explains function: the active site of an enzyme, the binding pocket for a drug, the misfolding in prion and amyloid diseases. Intrinsically disordered regions function without a fixed structure.

example.q: X-rays of wavelength 1.54 Å diffract at θ = 30° (first order, n = 1). What is the lattice spacing d?

analogies.tech: Folding is like water running down a funnel: many starting points, one low point.
analogies.home: Origami: a flat paper (sequence) folded along set creases gives one shape.
analogies.city: Crystallography is like reconstructing a building from the shadows cast from many angles.

stages.mnemonic: Primary line, secondary coil and sheet, tertiary fold, quaternary team.
terms: Tendency of nonpolar groups to cluster away from water, driving folding.
Local regular patterns such as α-helix and β-sheet.
Electron microscopy of frozen, hydrated molecules.
Protein that helps others fold correctly.

misc.wrong: A protein structure is a single rigid shape.
misc.right: Proteins are dynamic; crystal or cryo-EM structures show an average or a snapshot, and some regions are intrinsically disordered.

stages.limits: Crystals may favour one conformation, and predictions give a single model, so they may miss alternative functional states.

trip.prompt: Find an example of an α-helix and a β-sheet in a ribbon diagram of a protein.

questions.q: Which force chiefly drives the burying of nonpolar residues in a protein core?
o: Hydrophobic effect
Covalent peptide bonding
Ionic bonding
Nuclear forces
questions.why: Water excludes nonpolar groups, favouring their clustering.

questions.q: Which bonds stabilise α-helices and β-sheets?
o: Hydrogen bonds between backbone groups
Disulfide bonds between side chains far apart
Peptide bonds along the chain itself
Phosphodiester bonds in the backbone
questions.why: Backbone N–H···O=C hydrogen bonds form the secondary structures.

questions.q: X-rays with λ = 1.54 Å diffract in first order from planes with d = 3.08 Å. Find sin θ.
A structure has a resolution of 2.5 Å. Express this in nanometres.
Cryo-EM is especially valuable for proteins that are hard to:
o: Crystallise
Sequence by standard methods
Translate in the cell
Denature by heating
questions.why: It needs no crystals.

questions.q: A single amino acid substitution in the core replaces a nonpolar residue with a charged one. The likely effect is:
o: Destabilisation or misfolding
Increased stability, always, in every case
No effect on any protein whatever
Conversion of the protein into DNA
questions.why: A buried charge is energetically unfavourable.

questions.q: Levinthal's paradox is resolved by the idea that:
o: Folding proceeds down an energy landscape via guided pathways
Proteins try every possible conformation in turn
Folding takes many years in the cell
Proteins never fold on their own at all
questions.why: Funnel-shaped landscapes limit the search.

questions.q: Order the levels of protein structure from simplest to most complex.
questions.why: Each level builds on the previous one.

questions.q: Match each method to what it is best suited for.
pairs: Small proteins and dynamics in solution
Model from sequence, to be validated
questions.why: Methods complement each other.

questions.q: Explain why a mutation far from the active site can still reduce an enzyme's activity.
questions.model: A distant mutation can destabilise the fold or alter the dynamics and conformation, so the active site shape or flexibility changes, reducing activity.
questions.why: Function depends on the whole 3D structure and its dynamics.

panel.q: A predicted structure has high confidence for a domain but low confidence for a linker. What is the best interpretation?
o: The linker may be flexible or disordered
The linker does not exist in the real protein
The domain prediction must be wrong
The prediction is always right everywhere
panel.why: Low confidence often signals disorder or alternative states.

panel.q: Amyloid diseases involve proteins forming:
o: Cross-β fibrils from misfolded proteins
New DNA strands made by the cell
Membrane pumps in the cell wall
Normal enzymes that work faster than usual
panel.why: Misfolded proteins can aggregate into ordered fibrils.

panel.q: A drug binds into a pocket of a viral protease and blocks its function. Why is a high-resolution structure useful?
o: It lets designers fit molecules to the pocket
It reads out the sequence of the virus
It removes the pocket from the protein
It makes the drug cheaper to produce automatically
panel.why: Structure-based drug design relies on geometry of the binding site.

teach.topic: Why proteins fold into a specific shape
teach.model: A protein's amino acid sequence determines how it folds. Nonpolar side chains tuck inside, away from water, and hydrogen bonds form helices and sheets. The chain follows an energy funnel to a stable shape, and that shape determines what the protein can do.

stages.title: Synthetic biology
stages.hook: Engineers build circuits from wires and chips. Could we build circuits from genes and proteins inside a living cell, and what should we worry about?
explain: Synthetic biology applies engineering principles of standard parts, abstraction and design–build–test–learn cycles to living systems. Parts such as promoters, ribosome binding sites, coding sequences and terminators are combined into genetic circuits. Early landmark circuits were the toggle switch and the repressilator, both reported in 2000. The toggle switch is a bistable circuit of two mutually repressing genes; the repressilator is a ring of three repressors that produces oscillations.

Circuits can implement logic. A NOR gate gives output 1 only when both inputs are 0, and NOR is functionally complete, so any logic can be built from NOR gates. Challenges include context dependence, burden on the host, noise, mutation and evolution of circuits. Cell-free systems and genome-scale projects push further: the JCVI-syn3.0 minimal cell was built with a synthetic genome of 473 genes. Applications include biosensors, biomanufacturing of drugs and materials, and engineered cells for therapy.

Biosafety and ethics are central: containment strategies, kill switches and dependence on synthetic nutrients; screening of DNA synthesis orders; dual-use research that could be misused; open-source and equitable access; and public engagement. Release of engineered organisms such as gene drives requires careful risk assessment and community consent.

example.q: A cell has two NOR gates in series: gate 1 takes inputs (0, 0); its output goes to both inputs of gate 2 (a NOR with tied inputs acts as NOT). What is the final output?

analogies.tech: BioBricks are like standard electronic components that plug together.
analogies.home: A kill switch is like a circuit breaker that cuts the power when something goes wrong.
analogies.farm: Biosensors in microbes can change colour when they detect a contaminant in water.

stages.mnemonic: Design, Build, Test, Learn: repeat, with safety at every step.
terms: Interconnected genes and regulators performing a designed function.
A bistable circuit of two mutually repressing genes.
A synthetic ring of three repressors that oscillates.
An engineered safeguard that causes cell death under defined conditions.

misc.wrong: Engineered cells behave exactly like electronic circuits.
misc.right: Biological parts are noisy, interact with the host and evolve, so designs must be tested in context and may change over time.

stages.limits: Reliable prediction of circuit behaviour is still hard; many designs need extensive tuning in each host.

trip.prompt: Find the toggle switch or repressilator and explain how feedback produces its behaviour.

questions.q: Which synthetic circuit was designed to oscillate?
o: Repressilator
Toggle switch
A simple promoter
A kill switch
questions.why: Three repressors in a ring produce oscillations.

questions.q: A toggle switch has two mutually repressing genes. How many stable states does it have?
o: Two
One
Three
None
questions.why: Either gene A or gene B is on, giving bistability.

questions.q: A plasmid has a copy number of 50 per cell. How many copies are in a culture of 2 × 10⁹ cells?
A circuit adds a metabolic burden that slows growth by 20%. A control doubles every 40 minutes. Assuming growth rate scales by 0.8, how long does the engineered strain take to double, in minutes?
questions.why: Rate falls to 0.8, so doubling time = 40 ÷ 0.8 = 50 min.

questions.q: NOR is called functionally complete because:
o: Any logic function can be built from NOR gates
It has only one input, so it is simple
It always outputs 1 whatever the input
It needs no inputs to work at all
questions.why: NOT, OR and AND can all be made from NOR.

questions.q: Why do engineered organisms often lose a burdensome circuit over generations?
o: Mutants that drop the burden grow faster and take over
Circuits are erased by light in the lab
DNA cannot be copied by the cells
Selection does not act on microbes in culture
questions.why: Evolution favours faster-growing variants.

questions.q: Order the steps of a design–build–test–learn cycle.
items: Design the genetic parts and circuit
Build the DNA and insert it into cells
Use results to improve the design
questions.why: Iteration improves the design.

questions.q: Match each safeguard to its aim.
questions.why: Layered safeguards reduce risk.

questions.q: Give two reasons why releasing an engineered organism into the environment demands more caution than using it in a closed fermenter.
questions.model: Released organisms can reproduce, spread and cannot be recalled, interact with native species and ecosystems, may pass genes to wild relatives or microbes, and can evolve. Communities should also be consulted.
questions.why: Environmental release is hard to reverse.

questions.q: Which engineered safeguard makes a strain unable to survive without a compound not found in nature?
o: Synthetic auxotrophy
Antibiotic resistance
Overexpression
Plasmid copy number increase
questions.why: The cell depends on a supplied synthetic nutrient, limiting survival outside the lab.

panel.q: A gene drive spreads an allele through a population faster than normal inheritance. Which governance step is most appropriate before a field release?
o: Staged testing, risk assessment and community consent
Immediate release into the wild
Secrecy about the whole project
Releasing without any monitoring afterwards
panel.why: Gene drives can be irreversible, so careful oversight is needed.

panel.q: A biosensor strain turns red when it detects arsenic in groundwater. Which factor is most important for use in villages?
o: Low cost, reliability and safe containment
Complexity that few people understand
Using the most expensive reagents available
Secrecy about how the strain works
panel.why: Practical deployment needs reliability, affordability and safety.

panel.q: The minimal cell JCVI-syn3.0 still has some genes of unknown function. What does this show?
o: Our understanding of even a minimal cell is incomplete
Genes are unnecessary for a cell to live
All of the functions are now known
The cell is not alive at all
panel.why: A substantial fraction of essential genes lacked known function.

teach.topic: How a genetic toggle switch works
teach.model: A toggle switch has two genes that each repress the other. If gene A is on, it shuts off gene B, which keeps A on. If B is on, it keeps A off. So the cell has two stable states, and a brief signal can flip it from one to the other and it will remember.

points.ask: How do you change its state?

stages.title: Regenerative biology
stages.hook: A salamander regrows a whole limb; a human regrows only a fingertip in children and heals others with a scar. What do regenerating animals do that we mostly do not?
explain: Regeneration restores lost tissue. Planarian flatworms regenerate from neoblasts, pluripotent stem cells found throughout the body. Axolotls form a blastema, a mass of progenitor cells at the wound that rebuilds the limb with the correct pattern. Mammals regenerate some tissues well (liver, intestinal lining, blood) but heal many others with scar tissue. Wound healing proceeds through haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling.

Stem cells self-renew and differentiate. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) were made in 2006 by Shinya Yamanaka by introducing four transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc) into mouse fibroblasts, with human iPSCs following in 2007. Organoids are three-dimensional tissue-like structures grown from stem cells; they model development and disease and help test drugs. Tissue engineering combines cells, scaffolds and signals.

Challenges include controlling differentiation, preventing tumours from undifferentiated cells (teratomas), immune rejection, delivering cells to the right place, scale-up and cost. Regulation and ethics address embryo use, informed consent for donated cells, and unproven clinics that sell untested treatments.

example.q: A culture of 1 × 10⁶ iPSCs doubles every 24 hours. How many cells after 7 days, ignoring limits?

analogies.tech: iPSC reprogramming is like restoring a computer to factory settings.
analogies.farm: Pruning a plant triggers new shoots from buds, which is a regeneration strategy from stem cell-like zones.
analogies.city: A blastema is a temporary building site with a blueprint for what to rebuild.

stages.mnemonic: Wound, Clot, Cleanse, Cover, Remodel: haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, remodelling.
terms: Mass of progenitor cells that rebuilds a lost structure.
Stem cell made by reprogramming a specialised cell.
A 3D culture that resembles an organ in structure and function.
A tumour containing multiple tissue types, from undifferentiated stem cells.

misc.wrong: Stem cell clinics offering cures are all proven treatments.
misc.right: Only a few stem cell therapies, such as bone marrow transplants, are well established; many clinics sell unproven treatments with real risks.

stages.limits: Findings from axolotls and planarians do not automatically transfer to mammals; mammals have different immune and scarring responses.

trip.prompt: Find the four reprogramming factors and say what iPSCs can be used for.

questions.q: Which cells enable whole-body regeneration in planarians?
o: Neoblasts
Neurons
Red blood cells
Osteoclasts
questions.why: Neoblasts are pluripotent stem cells.

questions.q: A blastema in a regenerating limb is:
o: A mass of progenitor cells at the wound
A scar left over after the wound closes
A bone formed in the stump
A blood clot that seals the cut
questions.why: It rebuilds the lost structure.

questions.q: iPSCs from a patient are used to make cells for that same patient. A major advantage is:
o: Reduced risk of immune rejection
No risk of tumours
No cost
They are always younger than the patient
questions.why: Autologous cells are genetically matched, although risks remain.

questions.q: A culture of 2 × 10⁵ cells doubles every 24 hours. How many cells after 5 days (ignoring limits)?
A patient needs 4 × 10⁸ cells. If each iPSC culture flask yields 5 × 10⁷ cells, how many flasks are needed?
Why do undifferentiated pluripotent cells risk forming tumours when transplanted?
o: They can proliferate and form many tissue types uncontrollably
They are dead cells that cannot function in the body
They lack DNA, so they cannot be controlled
They cannot divide, so they stay small in the body
questions.why: Remaining undifferentiated cells can form teratomas.

questions.q: Order the phases of wound healing.
questions.why: Healing moves from clotting to tissue rebuilding.

questions.q: Match each approach to its description.
questions.why: Different strategies in regenerative medicine.

questions.q: Why can a salamander regrow a limb while a human forms a scar?
questions.model: Salamanders form a blastema by dedifferentiating cells and use positional signals to rebuild the pattern, with a regenerative immune response. Mammals tend to seal wounds with fibrotic scar tissue and lack a blastema-based programme.
questions.why: Differences in cell plasticity, signalling and immune response underlie regeneration.

questions.q: Which cell types did Yamanaka's original 2006 experiment reprogram to iPSCs?
o: Mouse fibroblasts
Human neurons grown in a dish
Red blood cells from an adult
Sperm cells from a male mouse
questions.why: The first iPSCs were derived from mouse fibroblasts with four factors; human cells followed in 2007.

panel.q: A clinic offers an expensive stem cell injection for a wide range of conditions with no published trial. What is the best response?
o: Ask for trial evidence and regulatory approval
Accept testimonials from past patients as proof
Pay in advance to secure a place
Assume it is safe because it is a clinic
panel.why: Unproven interventions can cause harm, so evidence is needed.

panel.q: Brain organoids are used to study development. Which ethical issue is discussed?
o: Whether complex organoids could gain features of consciousness or need protections
Whether they are alive when left in the sun
Whether they are really plants
None, since they contain only DNA and nothing else
panel.why: As organoid complexity grows, ethics boards consider limits.

panel.q: Why do liver cells regenerate better than heart muscle cells after injury in humans?
o: Hepatocytes can re-enter the cell cycle, whereas adult cardiomyocytes divide very little
The liver is bigger, so it has more cells to spare
Hearts have no cells that can be damaged
Livers have no blood supply that can be hurt
panel.why: Cell-cycle capacity differs between tissues.

teach.topic: What iPSCs are and why they are useful
teach.model: Induced pluripotent stem cells are made by adding a few transcription factors to a specialised cell, such as a skin cell, which resets it to a stem cell state. These cells can become many tissues, so scientists can study diseases, test drugs, and possibly grow replacement cells matched to a patient.

stages.title: Computational biology
stages.hook: A diagnostic test is 90% sensitive and 95% specific, yet a positive result may be wrong most of the time. How can computation and probability reveal why?
explain: Computational biology builds and tests models of biological data. Algorithms use dynamic programming for sequence alignment: the Needleman–Wunsch algorithm finds the best global alignment by filling a matrix with scores for matches, mismatches and gaps. Smith–Waterman does the same for local alignments. Scoring example: match +1, mismatch −1, gap −2.

Dynamic systems are simulated by numerical integration. Euler's method updates X(t + Δt) = X(t) + Δt × f(X); it is simple but accurate only for small steps. Stochastic simulation (the Gillespie algorithm) models random reaction events, important for small molecule numbers. Hidden Markov models predict genes and protein domains by modelling hidden states that emit observed symbols. Machine learning classifies samples, but needs separate training and test sets, cross-validation and caution about overfitting and bias in training data.

Probability thinking is essential. Bayes' theorem: P(disease | positive) = sensitivity × prevalence ÷ [sensitivity × prevalence + (1 − specificity) × (1 − prevalence)]. When prevalence is low, even good tests give many false positives. Reproducible code, version control and open data allow others to check the analysis.

stages.title: Advanced evolutionary genetics
stages.hook: The sickle cell allele is harmful in two copies, yet common where malaria has been prevalent. How can natural selection maintain a harmful allele, and how can genomes reveal the history of selection?
explain: Population genetics tracks allele frequencies. Selection with relative fitnesses w acts on heritable variation. With heterozygote advantage, fitness of AA = 1 − s, Aa = 1 and aa = 1 − t, the allele frequency settles at a stable equilibrium p̂ = t ÷ (s + t) for allele A. Directional selection raises a beneficial allele; purifying selection removes deleterious ones; balancing selection maintains variation.

Drift dominates in small populations. A new neutral mutation in a diploid population of size N has fixation probability 1 ÷ (2N). Heterozygosity declines by a factor of (1 − 1/(2N)) per generation. The effective population size Nₑ is often much smaller than the census size. Gene flow homogenises populations; the fixation index F_ST measures differentiation between them. Under the neutral theory, the substitution rate equals the mutation rate, which underlies the molecular clock: T ≈ d ÷ (2μ) for two lineages diverging with d substitutions per site and per-lineage rate μ.

Signatures of selection include an excess of nonsynonymous over synonymous changes (dN/dS > 1), reduced diversity around a recently swept allele (selective sweep), and high differentiation. Coalescent theory looks backward: for two lineages in a diploid population of constant size N, the expected time to a common ancestor is about 2N generations. Human genetic variation is mostly within rather than between continental groups, about 85–90% of total diversity, which is why race is not a biologically sharp category.

example.q: With heterozygote advantage, AA has fitness 0.9 (s = 0.1) and aa has fitness 0.6 (t = 0.4). Find the equilibrium frequency of A.

analogies.sport: Drift is like a short series of coin flips deciding who wins: small samples swing widely.
analogies.city: A mutation's fixation chance is like one lottery ticket among 2N tickets.
analogies.music: The molecular clock is a metronome of mutations, ticking at an approximately regular rate.

stages.mnemonic: Small N, big drift; heterozygote advantage balances; sweeps erase variation.

Loss of nearby variation as a beneficial allele spreads.
Ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rates.
Backward-in-time model of how lineages merge in common ancestors.

misc.wrong: Natural selection always removes harmful alleles completely.
misc.right: Recessive harmful alleles persist at low frequency, and heterozygote advantage can maintain them at high frequency.

stages.limits: Molecular clocks need calibration and rates vary among lineages, so divergence dates are estimates with uncertainty.

trip.prompt: Find the sickle cell example of heterozygote advantage and the geography of malaria.

Strong purifying selection removing changes
Neutral evolution with no selection at all
No mutation in the gene across species

o: It declines because of drift in the bottleneck
It rises because of the bottleneck itself
It is unaffected by the crash in numbers
It converts to RNA in the survivors

o: A recent selective sweep
Higher mutation everywhere
Random mating
Gene duplication only

o: Unequal reproduction, uneven sex ratios and fluctuations reduce it
Census counts are always wrong by a fixed amount
Nₑ counts only the males in the population

questions.why: Hitchhiking reduces nearby variation.

questions.why: Evolutionary forces act in different ways.

questions.q: Explain why the sickle cell allele can be common in regions with endemic malaria even though two copies cause disease.
questions.model: Carriers with one copy are partly protected against severe malaria, giving heterozygote advantage, while people with two copies suffer sickle cell disease. Balancing selection maintains the allele at an intermediate frequency where malaria is common.

Groups are genetically distinct species
There is almost no variation in humans at all
Variation is only caused by the environment

Discard the fossils and keep only the pedigree rate
Ignore the pedigree data and keep the fossil rate
Pick whichever rate they like better and move on
panel.why: Different clocks rely on different assumptions.

panel.q: Why does a harmful recessive allele persist at low frequency?
o: Selection acts weakly on heterozygotes that carry it
It is never selected against in any case
Mutation does not occur in that gene
It persists because it is a dominant allele

teach.topic: How genetic drift differs from natural selection
teach.model: Natural selection is non-random: alleles that improve survival or reproduction become more common. Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies from chance in who reproduces. Drift matters most in small populations, where chance can even remove helpful alleles or fix harmful ones.

stages.title: Integrative neuroscience
stages.hook: We can describe a neuron in exact equations but cannot yet say how billions of them make a thought. How do neuroscientists connect molecules, circuits and behaviour?
explain: Neuronal signalling can be modelled. Passive membrane properties give the length constant λ, so a subthreshold voltage decays with distance as V(x) = V₀·e^(−x/λ). Synaptic inputs are integrated over space and time; a neuron fires when depolarisation at the axon initial segment reaches threshold. Conduction velocity is roughly 1 m/s in unmyelinated thin axons and up to about 100 m/s in large myelinated ones.

Plasticity underlies learning. Long-term potentiation (LTP) depends on NMDA receptors acting as coincidence detectors: they open when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic cell is depolarised, letting Ca²⁺ in. Spike-timing-dependent plasticity strengthens synapses when presynaptic spikes precede postsynaptic ones. Dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error: firing increases for unexpected reward and dips when an expected reward is omitted. Neural oscillations coordinate activity across brain regions.

Methods differ in scale and resolution: patch clamp (single cell, ms), electrophysiology, calcium imaging and optogenetics (cell-type control with light), fMRI (whole brain, seconds, measures blood oxygenation, an indirect signal) and EEG (millisecond timing, poor spatial resolution). The neural basis of consciousness is a contested area with several competing theories. Findings from animals must be interpreted carefully, and human studies need informed consent and privacy protections.

teach.topic: How synapses can strengthen with learning
teach.model: At some synapses, an NMDA receptor opens only when glutamate is bound and the receiving cell is already depolarised. Calcium then flows in and starts signals that make the synapse stronger, which is long-term potentiation. So connections that are active together become stronger, which is a basis for learning and memory.

stages.title: Integrated life-sciences research project
stages.hook: You are given a research question: does a new fertiliser boost crop yield, and is the effect worth the cost? How do you design, run, analyse and report a study people can trust?
explain: A research project begins with a focused, testable question and a hypothesis, followed by a literature review. Design choices include controls, randomisation, blinding, replication and sample size. Statistical power is the probability of detecting a true effect; for comparing two means with equal groups, n per group ≈ 2(z_α/2 + z_β)² σ² ÷ δ², where σ is the standard deviation and δ the difference to detect. With α = 0.05 (z = 1.96) and power 80% (z = 0.84), (1.96 + 0.84)² ≈ 7.84.

Analysis should be planned in advance (preregistration) to avoid p-hacking and selective reporting. Report effect sizes and confidence intervals: the standard error is σ ÷ √n, and an approximate 95% interval is mean ± 1.96 × SE. For 2×2 outcomes, relative risk compares probabilities, and the odds ratio compares odds. Correct for multiple comparisons, check assumptions, and distinguish statistical from practical significance. Reproducibility depends on clear methods, shared data and code, and transparent reporting of negative results.

Ethics and safety are integral: animal research follows the 3Rs (replace, reduce, refine); human research needs informed consent, independent ethical review and privacy protection; biosafety levels (BSL-1 to BSL-4) set containment for pathogens; dual-use risks and environmental impacts are assessed. Fair authorship, honest data handling, and inclusion of local and Indigenous knowledge and communities where relevant are marks of research integrity. Conclusions should match the evidence and state limitations.

Publicly recording a study plan before collecting data.

Letting patients choose their group
Using only healthy volunteers
Stopping when the result looks good

o: p-hacking (selective reporting)
Good practice that gives reliable results
Preregistration of the study plan
A power calculation before the study

o: The result is suggestive and needs replication with a larger sample
The effect is definitely real and also large
The treatment is safe for all patients
The null hypothesis has now been proven true
questions.why: Wide intervals show imprecision.

Reduction
Refinement

Collect and analyse data as planned
questions.why: A plan is made and approved before data collection.

questions.q: Match each term to its definition.

A third variable linked to both cause and outcome
Others can obtain the same results from the same data and methods

questions.q: A fertiliser trial finds a statistically significant 1% yield increase. The fertiliser costs 10% of the crop's value. Evaluate the result.
questions.model: The result may be statistically significant but the 1% effect is small and does not cover the 10% cost, so it has no practical or economic value. Significance does not mean importance.
questions.why: Distinguish statistical from practical significance.

panel.q: A study uses data from a community that is not told how it will be used. What ethical principle is breached?
o: Informed consent and respect for the community
Randomisation of the people into groups
Blinding of the researchers to the groups
Replication of the study by others
panel.why: Participants and communities must understand and agree to uses of data and samples.

o: High containment, such as BSL-3 or BSL-4 as assessed
BSL-1 open bench work with gloves only
No containment, as the lab is clean
Any cupboard that can be locked is enough
panel.why: Containment must match the risk of the agent.

panel.q: A result fails to replicate in an independent lab. What is the most scientific response?
o: Investigate differences in methods and sample, and update beliefs
Hide the failure so the paper stays cited
Blame the other lab without checking their methods
Delete the original data so nobody can compare
panel.why: Failed replication is information about the claim and its conditions.

teach.topic: How to plan a trustworthy experiment
teach.model: Start with a clear question and hypothesis. Use a control group, randomise who gets which treatment and, where possible, blind participants and analysts. Decide the sample size with a power calculation and the analysis before collecting data. Then report the effect size and uncertainty honestly, share methods and data, and follow ethical rules.
